payload.markdown: Encapsulation promotes decoupling, which promotes reuse. Components that are self-sufficient and communicate with wider systems only through their public interface can often be moved from one system and used in another without change.

blocks.text: Encapsulation promotes decoupling, which promotes reuse. Components that are self-sufficient and communicate with wider systems only through their public interface can often be moved from one system and used in another without change.

payload.markdown: In fact, this is rarer than you might think. Even nicely orthogonal code can be project specific. When creating a set of classes for managing the content of a particular website, for example, it is worth taking some time in the planning stage to look at those features that are specific to your client and those that might form the foundation for future projects with content management at their heart.

payload.markdown: Another tip for reuse: Centralize those classes that might be used in multiple projects. Do not, in other words, copy a nicely reusable class into a new project. This will cause tight coupling on a macro level, as you will inevitably end up changing the class in one project and forgetting to do so in another. You would do better to manage common classes in a central repository that can be shared by your projects.

items: Classes & Objects: A class defines state and behaviour; objects are instances of that definition.
Coupling: How much one class leans on another's internals; good design keeps it low.
Encapsulation: Bundling state with the methods that touch it, and hiding the rest.
Interfaces: A pure contract of method signatures with no implementation.
Abstract Classes: A partial base class that forces subclasses to complete certain methods.
UML Class & Sequence: Standard diagrams for static structure and runtime interaction.
Unit of Work: Tracking changes to many objects and writing them in a single transaction.
